{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Gerald J. Dolan''' (27 March 1945 in [[Philadelphia]] – 17 June 2008 in [[Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania]]) was an American solid state physicist.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?dolang|title= Gerald Dolan|website= Array of Contemporary American Physicists|access-date= 2016-04-05|archive-date= 2016-04-26|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160426104044/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?dolang|url-status= dead}}<br>- {{cite journal |url=http://scitation.aip.org/content/aip/magazine/physicstoday/news/10.1063/PT.4.1989 |title=Obituary. Gerald Dolan |journal=Physics Today |year=2008 |doi=10.1063/PT.4.1989 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Education and career==
Dolan received his bachelor's degree in physics in 1967 from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and his Ph.D. in 1973 from [[Cornell University]] under John Silcox. As a post-doctoral researcher, he was at the [[State University of New York at Stony Brook]] (SUNY) under [[James Lukens|J. E. Lukens]], doing research on thin-film superconductors  from 1973 to 1976. From 1976 to 1987, he was at [[Bell Labs]] where he worked under the supervision of [[Theodore A. Fulton]] and then, from 1987 to 1989, at IBM's [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]]. From 1989 to 1996, he was a professor{{ambig|date=July 2022}} at the University of Pennsylvania. In 1996, he became a consultant in medical physics for Immunicon Corporation. He was briefly a guest researcher at the [[University of Twente]].

Dolan was a pioneer in the development of small tunnel junction circuits for the study of solid-state quantum phenomena and for the observation of individual electrons. In 1987, he developed with Theodore A. Fulton at Bell Laboratories the first [[single-electron transistor]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Fulton, T. A.|author2=Dolan, G. J.| title=Observation of single-electron charging effects in small tunnel junctions| journal=Physical Review Letters| volume=59| issue=1| year=1987| pages=109–112| doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.109|bibcode = 1987PhRvL..59..109F| pmid=10035115}}</ref> In the last part of his career, he worked on medical applications.

In 1987, he was elected a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] "for development of new techniques for fabricating microstructures and for contributions to our understanding of the physics of these microstructures".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1987&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=APS|access-date= 26 September 2020}}</ref>

In 2000, he received, with Theodore A. Fulton and [[Marc A. Kastner]], the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] for "pioneering contributions to single electron effects in mesoscopic systems".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/units/dcmp/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Gerald&last_nm=Dolan&year=2000 |title=Gerald J. Dolan|publisher=Division of Condensed Matter Physics. Prizes & Awards}}</ref>
